value.overview: The Wood Stork (Mycteria americana) is a large New World stork and one of the most distinctive wading birds in the Americas. It has a white body, black flight feathers, a long thick bill, and a bare, dark head and neck. Wood Storks live in freshwater and brackish wetlands, where they feed in shallow water. In Costa Rica, they are associated mainly with lowland wetlands, river basins, marshes, lagoons, and coastal habitats.
value.classification: The Wood Stork belongs to the stork family Ciconiidae and the genus Mycteria. It is the only Mycteria species found in North and Central America.
value.identification: Adults are large, long-legged birds measuring roughly 90–115 cm in length, with a wingspan of about 150–165 cm. The body is mainly white, while the flight feathers and tail are black. The featherless head and upper neck are gray to black, and the heavy bill is dark and slightly downcurved. Juveniles have a less strongly patterned head and a paler bill. In flight, the Wood Stork holds its neck and legs extended and often soars in groups.
value.rangeHabitat: Wood Storks range from the southeastern United States through Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and much of South America. In Costa Rica, they occur in lowlands on both slopes, especially around the Tempisque River basin and other wetlands of Guanacaste, as well as Caño Negro and the Río Frío region in the north. They use marshes, shallow lagoons, flooded savannas, mangroves, estuaries, ponds, rice fields, and forested wetlands for feeding, roosting, and nesting. Important Costa Rican sites include Palo Verde and nearby wetlands.
value.migrationStatus: Wood Storks are generally nonmigratory, but they make local and regional movements in response to water levels and prey availability. Costa Rican birds may range between wetland complexes and coastal lowlands rather than following a fixed long-distance migration route.
value.breeding: Wood Storks breed colonially, usually nesting in trees standing in or beside shallow water. Both adults help build a platform nest from sticks, and the female generally lays several eggs. The parents share incubation and feeding duties, bringing regurgitated food to the chicks. Colonies may include many nests and can be vulnerable to disturbance, falling water levels, and changes in wetland conditions. In Costa Rica, documented breeding has included colonies in the Tempisque drainage, including Isla Pájaros and other sites in Guanacaste, as well as the Río Frío area.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small fish, but also includes amphibians, aquatic invertebrates, reptiles, and occasionally small mammals. Wood Storks feed by wading through shallow water with the bill partly open and using sensitive touch to detect prey. When contact is made, the bill snaps shut rapidly. They feed most effectively where falling or fluctuating water levels concentrate fish and other aquatic animals in shallow pools.
value.behavior: Wood Storks are social birds that roost, forage, soar, and nest in groups. They often spend long periods standing quietly in shallow water, then move slowly while probing with the bill. Adults and juveniles frequently soar on rising air currents, sometimes forming large, loose flocks. They are usually quiet away from colonies, where nestlings and adults may produce low calls, bill-clattering, or other sounds during interactions.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered generally stable to increasing, although trends differ among regions and local colonies.
